prose:
# Review intents where the agent works, understand every screen, and see the feature map and the code before and after

Intents are reviewed before any code exists, so the review has to come to the reviewer the moment there is
something to review, and every part of it has to say what it is. The review therefore opens inside Claude Code, in
the Lastro pane, by itself whenever a proposal has intents waiting; the web app stays the place where a team reviews
together. Both explain each thing they show, and both add a map of the features and how they depend on each other,
and what the implementation did to the code: the cyclomatic complexity of its functions and the dependencies between
its modules, before and after. None of this judges the code: proofs stay the only verdicts, and the new views are
evidence for the reviewer.

## Reviewing in the Lastro pane

The Lastro pane in Claude Code (the board mod) opens by itself, with the keyboard on it, whenever the current
proposal has intents or decisions waiting for the reviewer, before the agent writes any code: right after the
intents are extracted, and again whenever a re-extraction or a derivation sends intents back to review. The reviewer
can close it; it opens again only when something new waits for them.

The pane shows the proposal's open decisions first, each with its options and the recommended one, then its
intents one at a time, each with the feature it changes, the feature's description before and after, the quote it
came from and the proofs approving it would replace. Buttons with keys answer a decision, approve an intent, amend
it (with a field for the new wording) or reject it (with a field for the reason), and after an amend or a reject
they rewrite the feature's description or ask for it to be recombined. Each press runs the same `lastro review`
command the chat review uses, as the reviewer, whose name comes from `LASTRO_REVIEWER` or git and is never an
agent's; the press is the reviewer's own act, so no permission prompt follows. The pane then moves to the next
item that waits, and says when nothing does.

While the pane is installed, the agent is told that the review happens there: it points the reviewer to the pane
instead of asking each decision and intent in the chat, and waits. Without the pane (in Codex, or with the mod not
installed) the chat review works as today.

The pane also has a Map view and a Code view that show, as text, the same feature map and code comparisons as the
web app below, for the current proposal.

## Understanding what is on the screen

Every part of the pane and of the web app says what it is. Each section starts with one sentence on what it shows
and what the reviewer does there (a decision is a question the extraction could not settle; an intent is one promise
of the change, on one feature; approving an intent that replaces proofs accepts that they stop guarding the old
behavior). Every badge and mark has an explanation on hover in the web app and in a legend the pane shows with `?`:
add, modify and remove; formal, empirical and beyond proof (and why proof stops there); the approvals count against
the policy; each proof verdict; and each state on the map and in the code views. A glossary page in the web app,
and the same text in the pane's legend, define proposal, intent, feature, decision, proof, regression, snapshot and
verdict in one sentence each. An empty view says why it is empty and what makes it fill.

## Reviewing intents in the web app

Every open proposal has an Intents tab, the one the app opens first while the proposal has intents to review. It
lists the proposal's intents in order, each with the feature it adds, modifies or removes, the feature's
description before and after as a word diff, the quote it came from, the proofs it replaces and its threads, and
the reviewer approves, amends or rejects each one there, as in the feature view. It filters to the intents that are
not settled or that wait for the reviewer, and the keyboard moves between intents (j and k) and opens approve,
amend and reject on the selected one (a, m and r).

A reviewer can approve every intent that waits for them at once; the app first says how many intents that is and
which proofs they replace, and approves only after the reviewer confirms. An amended or rejected intent is never
approved that way.

The header shows how many intents wait for the reviewer across every open proposal, and links to an inbox that
lists them grouped by proposal, oldest proposal first.

## The feature map

A Map page draws every feature as a node and every dependency as an arrow from the feature to the one it depends
on, from the features' surfaces and dependencies (proposal P-006). Features are laid out in columns by how deep
their dependencies go, in a deterministic order, so the same workspace always draws the same map. Each node shows
the feature's name, its surfaces and the state of its proofs: every proof passed, some only evidenced, one failing,
or no proofs. A feature with no surface is drawn as not reachable by a driver. A dependency on a feature that does
not exist or was removed, and every dependency cycle, are drawn in red and listed above the map with the features
they involve.

The map can show one proposal: the features it adds, modifies and removes are colored by change, the features that
depend on them, directly or not, are marked as affected, and the others fade. A proposal's page links to its map.
Clicking a feature opens its page, which lists what it depends on and what depends on it. The map can be filtered
by text.

## The code before and after

Two more snapshot kinds, taken like the other snapshots of a proposal (before when it is extracted, on the current
code; after when it is proved, on the new code) but for the repository's code rather than one intent's feature, so they
live with the proposal's repository-wide snapshots, in `.lastro/docs/<proposal>/repository/before|after/`
(`complexity.json` and `imports.json`). They are committed with the proposal and the proposal records the SHA-256 of
each one.

- complexity: the cyclomatic complexity of every function in the repository's source files: one plus its decision
  points (each if, loop, case, catch, conditional expression and short-circuit operator). TypeScript and JavaScript
  are read with a parser; Rust, Go and C# with a scanner that skips comments and strings. Files in other languages
  are listed as not measured.
- imports: the dependency graph between the repository's source files: an arrow for every import that resolves to
  another file of the repository (relative and workspace imports in TypeScript and JavaScript, `mod` and `use crate`
  in Rust, packages of the same module in Go). Files whose imports cannot be resolved are listed as not mapped.

Which files count follows `.gitignore` and the `code` section of `.lastro/config.json` (paths to include and to
exclude), and the same files give the same snapshot on every machine.

The comparison of a complexity pair lists every function added, removed or whose complexity changed, with its
file, before, after and difference, and each file's total and highest complexity before and after. A function above
the threshold (`code.complexityThreshold`, 10 by default) is marked, and one that crossed it in this proposal is
flagged. The comparison of an imports pair lists the arrows added and removed, the files added and removed, how
many files each changed file imports and is imported by, before and after, and every import cycle the change
introduced, by its files. Neither comparison blocks a proposal. The TypeScript, Go and .NET SDKs take and compare
these snapshots with identical results, like the other snapshot kinds.

## Seeing it in the app

A proposal has a Code tab. It shows the complexity comparison as a table of changed files that opens into their
functions, sortable by difference, and the imports comparison as a graph of the changed files and the files next to
them, with added arrows in green, removed ones dashed in red and new cycles highlighted. Until the proposal is
proved, the after side is taken from the working tree each time the page loads and is labeled as not yet
snapshotted, so reviewers can follow the implementation while it is written.

decisions.name: How much code the before snapshot covers
decisions.question: At extraction no one knows yet which files the change will touch. Should the before snapshot cover every source file, or only the paths listed in the code section of config.json?

options.label: Every source file, narrowed by config
options.consequence: Any file the implementation touches has a before; large repositories pay a full scan at every extraction unless they set include paths.

options.label: Only configured paths
options.consequence: Fast on any repository, but a repository without a code section gets no code snapshots at all.

decisions.name: Where the code snapshots are computed
decisions.question: Should the complexity and imports snapshots be computed by every SDK (TypeScript, Go, .NET) like the other snapshot kinds, or only by the TypeScript SDK for the review app?

options.label: Every SDK, identical results
options.consequence: Consistent with P-006 snapshots and the repo's parity rule; the Go and .NET ports need a TypeScript parser equivalent and cross-check tests, so the change is several times larger.

options.label: TypeScript SDK only
options.consequence: Ships much sooner; the snapshots are evidence that changes no verdict, so the CLIs in Go and .NET would skip them and say so, breaking parity for this one feature.

notPromised: The receipt does not get a Code section in this proposal (P-006 and P-007 already change the receipt).
Complexity and imports never become proofs or verdicts, and no threshold fails a proposal.
No code-to-feature mapping: the map links features to features, not to the files that implement them.
Languages other than TypeScript, JavaScript, Rust, Go and C# are not measured, and C# imports are not mapped.
The feature map's data (surfaces, dependsOn, affected) comes from P-006; this proposal only draws it.
The review app's existing behavior (described in .lastro/proposals/review-app.md) is not added to the catalog here.
The web app is not embedded in Claude Code: the pane is its own text interface over the same SDK commands.
In Codex, which has no mods, the review stays in the chat.
